entries.title: CNCF Research Shows Virtual Machines Remain Central as AI Workloads Evolve
entries.summary: New research from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and Linux Foundation Research finds that VMs host an average of 53% of production applications, while emerging AI and agentic workloads are creating additional demand for virtualisation, particularly where stronger execution isolation is required. By Craig Risi
entries.content:
Virtual machines (VMs) continue to account for a substantial share of cloud-native production infrastructure, despite the widespread adoption of containers and Kubernetes. New research from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and Linux Foundation Research finds that VMs host an average of 53% of production applications, while emerging AI and agentic workloads are creating additional demand for virtualisation, particularly where stronger execution isolation is required.

The report surveyed 492 cloud-native practitioners and technology leaders in September 2026. Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 34% identified AI and agentic workloads as a contributing factor. The findings suggest that rather than replacing virtual machines with containers, organisations are increasingly combining the two to accommodate different application and security requirements.

The research challenges the assumption that cloud-native adoption necessarily means moving away from virtual machines. While containers provide portability and efficient application packaging, VMs continue to offer isolation and support for workloads that depend on dedicated operating systems or established virtualisation environments.

The survey found that 51% of respondents run at least half of their production applications on VMs. This rises to an average of 64% in organisations with more than 10,000 employees, compared with 45% among organisations with fewer than 500 employees.

Furthermore, 71% of respondents who provided both current and expected workload figures anticipate their VM share remaining within the same range over the next year. This points towards continued coexistence rather than a wholesale migration to one deployment model.

One of the more significant findings concerns the relationship between AI adoption and infrastructure security.

AI agents increasingly generate and execute code, interact with tools, and access external systems. This creates new risks when generated code is executed in environments containing sensitive data or shared infrastructure.

Virtual machines offer a stronger isolation boundary than conventional containers, which share the host operating system kernel. The report identifies hardware-level VM isolation, containers running inside VMs, and MicroVM sandboxing as approaches organisations are using to contain AI workloads.

Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 47% cited security and isolation as a contributing factor, while 34% specifically identified AI and agentic workloads.

The survey also points to growing interest in stronger isolation technologies. MicroVM sandboxing adoption is expected to increase from 20% current use to 30% planned use, while confidential computing is expected to grow from 12% to 26%. These figures represent reported intentions rather than confirmed deployments.

Some 61% of respondents described their VM and container administration teams as collaborative or fully integrated, suggesting that managing different workload types is increasingly becoming a shared platform engineering responsibility.

Kubernetes is also beginning to play a role in virtual machine management. Among respondents using VMs, 8% reported using KubeVirt, the CNCF project that allows virtual machines to be managed through Kubernetes resources and APIs.

This brings VM lifecycle management into existing Kubernetes operational practices without requiring applications to abandon their virtualised environments.

The findings reinforce a shift in how cloud-native infrastructure is evolving. Kubernetes and containers remain important, but they are not necessarily the right execution model for every workload.

Technologies such as KubeVirt and Kata Containers show how virtualisation can integrate with container orchestration, while MicroVMs provide lightweight environments to isolate short-lived or potentially untrusted workloads.

For platform engineering teams, the research highlights the need to accommodate different execution environments without fragmenting operational practices. AI adds another dimension, making isolation, resource utilisation and workload security increasingly important infrastructure considerations.

The survey was sponsored by CNCF and Broadcom, and its results should be read as reported industry perspectives rather than a complete census of cloud-native deployments. Nevertheless, its findings provide a useful indication of where infrastructure priorities are moving.

entries.title: OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando
entries.summary: OpenAI has detailed Pando, a new backend that scales Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads without replacing familiar Git workflows. The company reports nearly 80% lower median push latency by coordinating branch updates independently and reusing stored packfiles across fetches. By Eran Stiller
entries.content:
OpenAI has detailed Pando, a new backend that scales Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads without replacing familiar Git workflows. The company reports nearly 80% lower median push latency by coordinating branch updates independently and reusing stored packfiles across fetches.

Pando now powers all development in OpenAI's monorepo and is serving nearly a petabyte of Git data per day. OpenAI attributes the increased load to Codex-driven development, and each push can in turn trigger multiple CI jobs that all fetch the same history. Pando went into production in April 2026.

Rather than replace Git's client and protocol, OpenAI has changed how the backend coordinates reference updates and stores and transfers objects. On a push, Pando validates the incoming packfile as it's being streamed to immutable blob storage, without unpacking it into a local repository. A metadata transaction records the reference version (containing the new branch tip, the packfile and its dependencies on earlier reference versions) and atomically updates the reference pointer. Updates to unrelated references can proceed independently of one another; updates to the same reference still need to be coordinated.

OpenAI refers to this as causal consistency with serialisable updates to individual references and read-your-own-write consistency. A reader gets the history needed for the requested revision, but fetching a number of branches won't provide a repository-wide snapshot. Two clients can see different combinations of branch versions during concurrent updates. The trade-off removes a shared coordination point for unrelated pushes.

Pando also changes how Git decides which objects to transfer. By default, when a client pushes a new feature branch, the server will advertise only a designated trunk branch as its base. That constrains the dependencies of the resulting packfile, which in turn allows Pando to reuse it for readers who already have that trunk history. Repeated or stacked branch pushes can resend objects outside trunk, trading some additional bandwidth for the benefit of reusable packs.



Pando’s topic-branch packs depend on advertised trunk history and can repeat objects from earlier pushes (source)

For fetches, Pando maps the client's existing and requested commits to reference versions and picks out the appropriate stored packs to cover the missing history. Git's packfile-uri capability allows the server to return download links rather than generate a bespoke pack for each client. Express, a regional pack-delivery cache, serves those downloads. OpenAI reports cache-hit rates in excess of 99% and tests in which clone and fetch operations saturated 10 Gbps network links.

Background compaction groups packs into larger, geometrically sized covers, resembling compaction in a log-structured merge-tree. The covers provide better compression and act as a skip-list-like index for fetch planning. Pando keeps packs at every level so that clients with different histories can still be served.



Pando groups successive packs into larger covers to improve compression and fetch planning, retaining packs at every level (source)

The design contrasts with Anthropic's Scion, previously covered by InfoQ. Scion replaces Git's underlying model with changesets recording files changed relative to their first parent and content-addressed pointers to compressed file contents; commits, merges, rebases and history queries run server-side. Its clients retrieve missing immutable trees and blobs, rather than negotiate Git packfiles, and use bounded local caches and sparse or virtualised checkouts.

Both systems make use of immutable data and regional caches to reduce repeated computation. The way in which they draw the compatibility line is very different, though. Pando preserves Git's object model and client-side workflows and changes the backend coordination and delivery. Scion, on the other hand, assumes an online client and moves the repository operations into a dedicated service. The improvements they report are not directly comparable. OpenAI reports on push latency, whereas Anthropic reports on checkout speedups and infrastructure reductions compared with its previous Git-based setup.

Git compatibility did not eliminate migration work. OpenAI initially deployed Pando as a read- and write-through proxy, moved clients in phases, and migrated hundreds of integrations using legacy APIs, webhooks and repository downloads. It also distributed its own Git build, which supports parallel downloading and indexing of independent packs. OpenAI says some client improvements are already upstream, with others available in its public repository.

For the architects, it's a case of two separate decisions: which source control operations go on the server and which of the consistency and transfer guarantees do the workloads actually need. Pando retains the Git workflows but dispenses with the repository-wide snapshot across branches and accepts redundant transfers in order to reduce the amount of coordination and per-fetch computation.

entries.title: Article: Engineering Around Non-Determinism: Evals, Grounding, and Release Gates for AI-Drafted Suspicious Reports
entries.summary: Moving GenAI into high-stakes production requires treating non-determinism as an engineering problem. This architectural blueprint shows engineering leaders and architects how to build trustworthy agentic workflows using knowledge graphs, dual-layer eval judges, CI/CD release gates, and regression testing against golden datasets to automate drafting while maintaining zero-hallucination compliance.
entries.content:
Key Takeaways

  • A drafting agent should refuse to draft when the evidence is missing. Stopping with an explicit "insufficient context" signal is safer than a fluent narrative built around gaps.
  • An LLM judge is itself non-deterministic. Freeze its version and pair it with a deterministic fact-checker for names, dates, and amounts.
  • Building agentic systems on probabilistic LLMs requires engineering around them: evals, context engineering, observability, regression runs, and human-in-the-loop controls contain the effects of randomness rather than removing it.
  • Grounding the system in authoritative case evidence and a knowledge-augmented graph data system helps ensure that every material claim is supported by traceable data.
  • Versioned models, prompts, policies, retrieval configurations, and reviewer actions make the system observable, reversible, and suitable for regulated production environments.

Investigative narrative drafting in a financial institution

Financial institutions must investigate potentially suspicious activity and prepare accurate, complete, and timely reports for Financial Intelligence Units. The process is sensitive, labor-intensive, and subject to strict deadlines. This article explains how non-deterministic Artificial Intelligence (AI) components can be incorporated into a dependable agentic system that reduces the cost of doing business, increases drafting and review speed, and maintains the quality of the final report.

What is a Suspicious Activity Report?

A Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) is a formal document submitted by regulated entities and financial institutions to law enforcement or financial intelligence units (such as the UK's National Crime Agency) to flag known or suspected instances of money laundering, fraud, or terrorist financing.

SARs should give a clear and concise explanation of the reason(s) for the suspicion, identifying:

  • Who – the identity of the party, or parties involved
  • What – the transaction they are involved in
  • Where – a description of the criminal property
  • How – a description of the prohibited act(s)
  • Why – the criminal activity suspected
  • When – any critical deadlines

The Inverted Pyramid Plot Model for SAR narratives organizes information from most to least important, much like a news article.

  • The narrative opens with the lead, a short summary of the most noteworthy details and the main story event.
  • It answers the five W questions: who, what, when, where, and why.
  • Next comes the body, a series of crucial details that build up the main story event, supported by evidence, facts, and patterns.
  • The narrative closes with the tail, which gives concluding remarks.

Because the structure moves from the broadest, most critical information down to the narrowest, a reader can grasp the core of the case from the opening lines alone and turn to the later sections only for supporting detail.

Risks and cost of non-compliance

  • Regulators penalize institutions for systematic data deficiencies, missing narratives, or failing to report suspicious transactions adequately.
  • Public enforcement actions can undermine the confidence of investors, business partners, and customers.
  • Considering the sensitivity of data and investigations, typically these cases are investigated and reported by in-house employees in a very secure environment. If suspicious activity volumes increase, the cost of investigation and reporting increases as well. For example, If there are 10% of active customers who are detected, investigated, and reported, and each case takes $50 in human labour cost, there is a significant increase in the cost of doing business, which has to be eventually passed back to the customer.

Typical Deterministic System Architecture

In the following system context diagram, a human agent views the investigation notes prepared by another human agent and then drafts the suspicious activity report. Once the report is reviewed by another peer, it is submitted to a financial intelligence unit.

System Context Diagram of Suspicious Activity Reports in a Financial Institution (Source: authors)

In the following diagram, there are 4 key timelines of any investigation:

  1. Detection: Any suspicious activity is detected either through manual oversight or with the support of machine learning models.
  2. Investigation: Once suspicious activity is detected, it goes for thorough investigation and peer review to confirm the suspicion.
  3. Reporting: Any confirmed suspicious activity has to be reported to the national financial intelligence unit within a tight deadline. The report has to be factually correct, and the suspicion has to be clearly articulated.
  4. Further investigation by the Financial Intelligence Unit: All of these suspicious reported activities by all financial institutions enable the national intelligence unit to understand the complete web of illicit activities and intervene before they become a threat to national or international security.

High-level diagram of a traditional reporting system (Source: authors)

  • The quality of the reports is directly proportional to the quality of investigation & editorial style of the human workforce. There is a lack of consistency.
  • If there is an increase in suspicious activities, then the manual system can not keep pace with the increase in demand.
  • There is a cost to the business and the customer for every suspicious activity investigation and reporting.

Non-Deterministic Agentic System Architecture

We propose improving the traditional reporting system by using AI to automate selected tasks and generate high-quality SAR drafts, followed by specialized human review and minor edits where necessary. The goal is to increase throughput, reduce cost per case, and decrease reporting failures.

In the following system context diagram, human agent effort is shifted to review/edit the AI-assisted report drafting and review.

System Context Diagram of Suspicious Activity Reports in a Financial Institution (Source: authors)

We changed the earlier design to support background automation of suspicious activity report generation. As soon as the investigation is complete, the case is sent to the queue for processing by the Agentic System. Before the human agent picks the case for drafting the report, the AI Agent has drafted the first version to speed up the report generation.

High-level diagram of an AI-powered reporting system (Source: authors)

The non-deterministic nature of AI, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), creates two central concerns:

  • High-quality first-attempt drafts require strong control, evaluation, and monitoring of AI components.
  • Low-quality drafts create repeated draft-and-review cycles and additional human editing, increasing the cost per report.

Multi-agent system for report generation

The proposed solution is a multi-agent system, with access to selected LLMs via a gateway, and supported by a tailored knowledge graph built from operational data.

Grounding is the foundation of trustworthy SAR generation. The system should make it easier to state only what the evidence supports, not merely make the prose more fluent.

High-level diagram of the agentic system (Source: authors)

  1. Preprocessed Event Plot Knowledge Graph: All the data is already tagged and collected by previous processes. There is an Event Plot Knowledge Graph already generated as part of detection and investigation.
  2. Data Query Planner Agent: fetches the quality data required to generate the report. If the data is not present, then we stop the agentic automation and give feedback to the user that Agents cannot generate the report as the data is not present.
  3. Data Reranker Agent: takes the data returned by Data Query Planner and re-ranks the data to ensure that data is relevant to the context.
  4. Drafter Agent: specialized agents produce a narrative from factual data, against a defined SAR schema, and cite supporting source identifiers.
  5. Judge Agent: deterministic checks and an independent judge assess factuality, completeness, consistency, and style.
  6. Coordinator Agent: Once the quality of the generated report is of decent standard, then the report is published for human review.
  • Since the investigation of the network is already done, there is no need for community detection. Hence, the GraphRAG approach is not considered.
  • We also need to ensure that security and privacy concerns of the cases are under consideration; hence, data is carefully labelled and collected.
  • All the real-time updates are present in operational databases, which can be fetched by the agents if there are some updates for a particular user profile or transaction.
  • Knowledge Graph of main and associate suspects are generated at a regular cadence through data pipeline jobs.
  • If a case is investigated and reported, then data needs to be retained as per data retention policies of the jurisdiction.

Sequence diagram of Drafter agent, Judge Agent and Human (Source: authors)

High-quality report generation with Evals

Quality means more than well-written prose. It means a complete, internally consistent, reviewable narrative that meets institutional and jurisdictional requirements.

  • Completeness against the required SAR narrative fields.
  • Consistency across names, dates, amounts, accounts, locations, and transaction sequences.
  • Clear separation of observed facts, analysis, and unresolved uncertainty.
  • Appropriate tone and terminology without overstatement or unsupported conclusions.
  • Traceable provenance for material statements and reviewer edits.

Unlike traditional software, LLM outputs are non-deterministic, and "quality" is subjective. In the case of report writing, "what does a good report look like?" becomes more subjective. Hence, there is a need to test the "subjective" aspects against "objective" metrics, and here the Eval shines.

Evals are like tests of regular software development practices, and they can be leveraged in the following processes:

  1. Initial development of the system
  2. Updates to the system when there is a change in the requirements
  3. Updates in the models
  4. Regular run on some percentage of production spans to assess overall drift in quality
  5. Any new release in any aspect of the AI system has to be gated with the Evals suite

Eval Creation

There are a few broad focus areas where the model output has to be tested on a continuous basis:

  • Instruction following capability
  • Generation capability
  • Narrative-specific correctness

For example, Evals can be written to assess different aspects of the generated narrative like:

  1. Factual accuracy of the narrative
  2. Factual completeness of the narrative
  3. Name identification
  4. Timeframe of events
  5. Narrative follows the Inverted Pyramid Plot structure
  6. Narrative Articulation
  7. Narrative Coherence
  8. Narrative tone
  9. ..etc.

Sample Eval can look like this:

Sample Eval (Source: authors)

Once we have scores from all the evals, either we can use a weighted average or a simple average of all the individual scores to figure out the final grading criteria. This is how the Evals can be leveraged to grade the quality of generated output

Sequence diagram of Evals grading (Source: authors)

Regression Evals with Golden Data Set

Since the model and prompt are bound to change, this adds another dimension of non-determinism to the system. With any production system, we need to have a regression run of all evals against the golden data set before any model upgrade or prompt/config change happens.

The golden data set has to be collected initially with different edge cases with defined input and output. This will help in testing the system during development. The Golden Data Set can be augmented with human feedback in production where they love the output generated by the AI system.

Evals shall answer some of the generated report’s quality metrics like :

  1. Did the system provide a factually correct answer?
  2. Was the summary faithful to the source?
  3. Was the final response actually helpful to the user?

System Behavior observability

Traditional testing is a deterministic process of verification - it asks, "Did we build the product right?" against a fixed specification. This approach fails when a system’s core logic is probabilistic, because non-deterministic output may be more likely to introduce subtle degradations of quality that do not result in explicit crashes and may not be repeatable. Hence, it is important to monitor the decision-making trajectory, from initial intent to final outcome.

  1. LLM Model: We first check the core reasoning. Is the LLM Model itself the problem? Failures here include hallucinations, nonsensical or off-topic responses.
  2. RAG Performance: The response depends on the quality of its retrieved information. Failures include irrelevant document retrieval, fetching outdated or incorrect information, or the LLM ignoring the retrieved context entirely and hallucinating an answer anyway.
  3. System Failures: What happens when the Model is not able to find the right context or data? Does it make things up or throw the error? What happens when the underlying system is unavailable?

The system is gradually improved by generating telemetry, understanding the system, and patching the underlying issues.

Human-in-The-Loop Control

Human review remains a policy decision owned by the BSA/AML function. AI accelerates preparation; it does not replace accountable judgment.

  • Risk-tiered routing: low-risk, familiar typologies may use sampling or streamlined review; novel, high-risk, multilingual, or low-confidence cases default to full review.
  • Reviewer experience: show evidence beside each material claim, highlight uncertainty, and make changes explainable rather than forcing reviewers to rewrite from scratch.
  • Review quality: evaluate human edits as well as AI output so reviewers correct errors without introducing unsupported statements.
  • Accountability: the designated BSA/AML officer retains responsibility for filing decisions and approved risk thresholds.

Release Process

Treat models and prompts as regulated production changes. The release plane provides controlled progress rather than "ship and hope."

  1. Version: register the model, prompts, retrieval logic, data mappings, policies, and eval set with an owner and change rationale.
  2. Test: run deterministic factuality checks, rubric scoring, security and privacy checks, and jurisdiction-specific regression suites.
  3. Gate: require approval from engineering, Compliance/AML, Risk, and Legal according to the change type.
  4. Shadow and canary: compare the candidate with the incumbent before increasing traffic.
  5. Monitor: track factuality pass rate, judge scores, reviewer edit rate, latency, queue age, and escalation volume.
  6. Rollback: use configuration-based feature flags to revert to the previous model, stricter review, or full human drafting when thresholds are breached.

Engineering Trust Into AI-Drafted SARs

The bottleneck in drafting a quality Suspicious Activity Report was qualified personnel. LLM-based systems can reduce that dependency, but only if they're engineered for it, with grounding and evals as the substitute for the judgment of a qualified investigator.

The mechanism we've described treats non-determinism as an engineering problem rather than an excuse. Grounding drafts in a case-specific knowledge graph and operational data keeps the Drafter Agent grounded in evidence. A Judge Agent and deterministic fact-checker turn "does this read well?" into measurable checks against factuality, completeness, and the Inverted Pyramid structure the FIU expects. Evals and a golden dataset give these subjective judgments an objective, regression-testable backbone, the same way unit tests do for deterministic code. And a release process that versions models, prompts, and configuration, gated with shadow/canary rollout and feature-flag rollback, treats every change to the system as a production release

None of this shifts accountability away from the humans who own it. The BSA/AML officer still decides what gets filed; the agentic system's job is to make sure that when a human reviews a draft, the evidence is already assembled, the uncertain claims are flagged, and the reviewer's time goes to judgment rather than transcription. Risk-tiered routing means the system earns trust on familiar, low-risk cases before it is ever allowed near the ones that matter most.

SAR narratives can now be drafted at machine speed, by codifying what "good" looks like into evals a machine can check against. When a human reviews the output, they're not taking the narrative on faith; they can trace the reasoning and the evidence lineage behind it, and that traceability is what turns speed into trust.

entries.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Lessons from Building a $100M Product in Six Weeks at OpenAI
entries.summary: At QCon San Francisco 2026, OpenAI's Brian Yang described building the ChatGPT ads product with Codex agents and no human-written code. He outlined layered testing, sandboxes, and batched pull request reviews, and noted failure modes such as code "slop" and unsafe agent actions. He advised gradual adoption and framed engineers as managers of agents. By Daniel Curtis
entries.content:
At QCon San Francisco 2026, Brian Yang, Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI, described how a small group of engineers used coding agents to build the ChatGPT ads product, reaching $100 million in annualised recurring revenue within six weeks of launch and $1 billion in under 200 days, with zero human-written code.

Yang, previously at Google, Meta and LinkedIn, was a founding member of technical staff on ChatGPT Ads, which was built entirely using Codex. His central claim was that software engineering is alive but reshaped around building the system that builds the product, with the engineer acting more as a manager of agents than a line-by-line contributor. One engineer can now triage an issue, open a pull request, write documentation and unblock CI in parallel, a shift Yang compared to multi-processing.

Every change runs local and unit tests, complex changes get end-to-end user journeys via browser automation, and the most critical changes run inside production-like sandboxes with representative traffic. Sandboxes come in three forms of read-only, write-only with telemetry suppressed, and full-fidelity with telemetry tagged using a shadow tag so it can be filtered out downstream. Yang's team targets around 90% auto-approval of everyday PRs, reviewing the past 300 to 400 PRs weekly and backtesting reviewer thresholds against that rate.

He illustrated the model with a sanitised latency study where candidate PRs targeted time-to-first-ad at P50 and P95 with guardrails for ads returned, timeouts and error rates. Candidates A and B passed; candidate C was rejected because the sandbox returned no ad. Thirty to forty candidates are typically bundled into one PR and run together for a day or two before human review, because changes that pass in isolation can regress when combined.

On failure modes, Yang described codebases filling with "slop" when agent output is unchecked, so maintenance agents sit alongside feature agents to root-cause newly appearing log patterns. Agents over-write tests, so he reviews the 50 slowest tests weekly. He recounted an agent that deleted and re-provisioned slow Kubernetes pods without asking, arguing that teams need big-company controls such as authorised roles for destructive actions and physical confirmation for deployments. Yang encouraged teams to revisit "cached assumptions" such as the belief that four nines of uptime always beats higher revenue, and recommended giving every engineer a monthly AI budget with no leaderboards.

For team adoption, Yang recommended a gradual path from automating one PR, to one feature, to one project, warning that jumping straight to project automation is where systems tend to break. For teams that are resistant to AI, he described rotating an "AI champion" every two weeks. The champion picks the team's most tedious recurring task, such as GPU provisioning at OpenAI which can take hours of babysitting, snapshots and permissions work, teaches an agent to do it end-to-end as a reusable skill, and demos the result at the end of the fortnight. Over a year, that converts 26 pain points into agent-owned workflows and gives sceptical engineers tangible value rather than abstract promises.

Day to day, Yang prefers Codex's bidirectional voice mode over typing for task intake, spending around ten minutes being interviewed by the agent about requirements before agreeing on a spec and handing it to multiple agents. He uses an orchestrator thread that spawns five sub-threads to explore different approaches in parallel and picks the strongest result, rather than copy-pasting the same prompt into several chats. On models, he switches only when a new release makes the workflow feel easier, with fewer clarifying questions and equivalent output quality, rather than chasing benchmark scores. His closing message was that engineers will increasingly do for agents what managers currently do for engineers, requiring an expansion of skills around direction-setting, architecture and verification rather than their replacement.

entries.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Securing AI Agents in Production
entries.summary: At QCon San Francisco, Google's Amanda Walker framed AI agents as an insider-risk problem operating at machine speed, and described identity, credential and containment patterns for running them safely in production. By Mark Silvester
entries.content:
Securing AI agents is a variation of the insider-risk problem, requiring distinct identities, narrowly scoped credentials and fine-grained policy controls, according to Amanda Walker, senior director of engineering for privacy, safety and security at Google. In a QCon San Francisco session, she outlined patterns for teams whose agents have been adopted organically and are running ahead of their security and observability frameworks.

With agents now executing multi-step plans in live production environments, Walker argued that "a rogue AI agent is the same problem as a rogue human insider," one that acts with superhuman speed and persistence. Controls therefore need to work at machine speed, rather than relying on someone reviewing logs the next morning. She covered identity and credentials, boundary defence, subagent orchestration and policy-based containment.

Walker described giving an agent raw human credentials as the fastest path to production failure. The agent inherits the user's authority, so a prompt injection in a document can turn that access to an attacker's purposes. She recommended explicit principals for agents, the AI equivalent of service accounts, so each agent can be provisioned and logged separately without impersonating anyone.

Scoped OAuth tokens limit an agent's access in time and scope, but are immutable once issued. With credential attenuation, an orchestrator instead mints narrower tokens for its subagents, such as read-only access to logs, or read-only access to a repository between two commits when bisecting a broken build.

She pointed to Eclipse Biscuit, a token format whose holders can append restrictions, but cannot remove existing ones without invalidating its signature. It takes more work than reusing human authentication infrastructure, but suits services where teams control both ends.

For API keys, a proxy can give the agent a short-lived synthetic key and substitute the real one as traffic leaves, protecting it from prompt injection and exfiltration.

Walker cautioned that a virtual machine protects the host, not the resources an agent can reach: an agent with network access can still delete a database. Container sandboxes, ephemeral runtimes and sidecar proxies such as Envoy give finer control over file system and network access. But "a perfectly isolated compute sandbox is not useful," she said, so teams need policies that constrain what agents do with the services they call.

She also highlighted poisoned skills on public marketplaces that steal API keys and cryptocurrency wallets, citing Snyk research that found more than a third of publicly available skills had at least one security flaw.

Agents also cause harm by being wrong rather than malicious. Walker described an agent that read internal SRE documentation and invoked a break-glass process intended for emergencies, having decided it was the most expedient route. Monitoring caught it, but the lesson was that organisations must distinguish agents from the people they work for, because some processes depend on a human accepting risk. For the same reason, she described computer-use agents, which drive a mouse and keyboard, as in essence impersonation, while acknowledging they solve problems that machine protocols such as MCP cannot.

Asked in the question-and-answer session about tagging identities as agents, Walker said: "The biggest thing it gave us was auditability about some of these risk decisions." The distinction supports human-only rules, such as emergency access, and can help with agent-only rules, such as signed releases in regulated environments, although she noted that an agent flag alone is not enough for those.

In the Q&A, she also advised security teams not to simply say no, which pushes colleagues to work around controls, but to allow experimentation where mistakes are reversible and keep human review for irreversible actions such as wire transfers.

entries.title: How LinkedIn Built a View-Agnostic Analytics System for Modern iOS UI Architectures
entries.summary: To address the challenge posed by modern iOS UI systems where the logical UI structure may not mirror the native UIKit hierarchy, LinkedIn engineers developed a view-agnostic analytics system build around a shared MeasurableNode contract. By Sergio De Simone
entries.content:
To address the challenge posed by modern iOS UI systems where the logical UI structure may not mirror the native UIKit hierarchy, LinkedIn engineers developed a view-agnostic analytics system build around a shared 

MeasurableNode
contract.

As LinkedIn senior software engineer Keerthana Reddy Ragi explains, while traditional iOS analytics relies on 

UIView
instances as the unit of measurement, modern UI architectures increasingly use flattened layouts and custom rendering systems where UI elements such as cards, sections, and containers are represented by virtual nodes that never materialize as 
UIView
s. Consequently, analytics systems built solely around UIKit may fail to capture impressions for virtual nodes, lose logical hierarchy and contextual information, miscalculate visibility and impression duration, and attribute user actions to the wrong elements.

LinkedIn's solution introduces a shared 

MeasurableNode
contract relaxing the requirement for every measurable element to be a 
UIView
. A 
MeasurableNode
exposes four properties: identity, geometry, hierarchy, and lifecycle.
protocol MeasurableNode: AnyObject { 
    var telemetryIdentity: TelemetryIdentity { get } 
    var frame: CRect { get } 
    var logicalParent: MeasurableNode? { get }
    var isAttached: Bool { get } 
    
    func attach ()
    fun detach)

As 

MeasurableNode
is a shared contract, both traditional 
UIView
s and virtual nodes can participate in the same analytics system. Indeed, while existing UIKit views continue using native UIKit properties and lifecycle hooks, virtual nodes explicitly provide the corresponding information to the same analytics layer.

The 

attach
and 
detach
methods are central to this approach, because they enable the layout or rendering system to notify the analytics system "when a node attaches, when its frame changes, and when it detaches". Unlike virtual nodes, UIKit already sends automatic lifecycle notifications to 
UIView
s. Similarly, as virtual nodes are not directly recognized by UIKit as gesture-recognizer targets, the rendering framework must traverse the hybrid UIKit/virtual-node parent hierarchy to attribute user actions to the appropriate logical virtual node.

Ragi emphasizes that this design enables gradual adoption without requiring existing view-based analytics to be rewritten.

Teams can modernize one part of the UI without rewriting everything around it. Existing view-based analytics can keep working while newer virtual nodes use the new contract.

LinkedIn engineers encountered three main challenges developing this approach to analytics. First, the widespread assumption that everything is a 

UIView
is embedded in existing codebases. For example, "helper code that walked superviews, visibility checks that read frames directly from views, cleanup logic tied to view removal". All these cases had to be found and updated. Second, they had to strike the right balance between short-term compatibility and long-term correctness. Third, they needed to enforce the attach/detach discipline at the framework level.

Commenting on Ragi's article on LinkedIn, senior AI prompt engineer Artien Nadal observed:

I think there's a bigger opportunity here than just making analytics independent of the UI. What if teams could automatically detect when a UI change breaks event tracking or changes what an event actually means?

As a final note, although LinkedIn's implementation focused on UIKit, the underlying approach is far from being limited to it. With many apps now mixing UIKit and SwiftUI, cross-platform layout engines, or hybrid solutions, a view-agnostic analytics model based on a shared contract has broader applicability.

entries.title: JEP 545 Moves ZGC Memory Preparation off the Startup Path in JDK 28
entries.summary: JEP 545, Faster Startup and Warmup with ZGC, has been integrated into JDK 28, moving heap memory preparation onto concurrent worker threads. ZGC now pre-touches memory as it expands and upgrades small pages to large ones on Linux 6.1 and later, but the 2 MB initial heap behind the JEP's 38% startup and 90% warmup gains requires the adaptive heap sizing flag from JEP 546, which is off by default. B
entries.content:
JEP 545, Faster Startup and Warmup with ZGC, has been integrated into JDK 28, moving the work of acquiring and preparing heap memory off the startup path and onto dedicated concurrent worker threads. On Linux 6.1 and later it also upgrades 4 KB pages to 2 MB pages while the application runs. The 2 MB initial heap behind the JEP's headline numbers comes from elsewhere: adaptive heap sizing, in the companion JEP 546, which still defaults to off.

Deploying ZGC has until now meant choosing which half of a trade-off to pay for. The collector's pause times do not grow with the heap, but its collection frequency does, so a small heap brings on early and frequent cycles. The JEP describes the older ergonomic behavior of committing one sixty-fourth of physical memory for the initial heap.

A team chasing fast startup set a tiny 

-Xms
and accepted a long warmup, because the collector then had to acquire and prepare memory in increments while the application was already allocating. A team chasing fast warmup set a large 
-Xms
, usually with 
-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch
, and paid the whole bill before the first request landed. The JEP puts the spread at roughly a tenth of a second to start with a 2 MB heap against more than ten seconds with a 32 GB one on current hardware.

That work now happens in a new thread, 

ZMemoryWorker
, one per heap partition. It commits and uncommits memory concurrently as capacity changes. It also heats memory before application threads reach it, which means pre-touching page by page and collapsing small pages into large ones.

The budget is fixed rather than adaptive. 

ZConcurrentWorkersCPUShare
in 
zGlobals.hpp
is 0.25, so preparation takes at most a quarter of the available CPU. ZGC's director caps young-generation worker counts when adaptive sizing is on, which keeps collection inside its CPU target while expansion continues and the collector deliberately runs above its heuristic heap size target.

Large pages on Linux no longer require an administrator to reserve them up front. ZGC probes for 

MADV_COLLAPSE
, the 
madvise
mode added in Linux 6.1, by mapping a 4 MB region, pre-touching a single page and collapsing an aligned 2 MB range. When the probe succeeds and memory heating is enabled, the collector enters a new 
Collapse
state and upgrades pages in the background. The call races the kernel's 
khugepaged
, so the implementation retries on 
EAGAIN
.

The change shows up in what a deployer no longer has to decide. Where JDK 25 forced a choice between two tunings, JDK 28 offers a third option:

JDK 25, tuned for startup

$ java -XX:+UseZGC -Xms2m -Xmx32g -jar app.jar

JDK 25, tuned for warmup

$ java -XX:+UseZGC -Xms32g -Xmx32g -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch -jar app.jar

JDK 28, neither trade-off

$ java -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZAdaptiveHeapSizing -jar app.jar

The third command produces the JEP's case study figures, a 38% drop in startup time and a fall in warmup from 80 seconds to 10 for Spring PetClinic on a 32 GB machine. 

-XX:+ZAdaptiveHeapSizing
takes the minimum and initial heap down to 2 MB and raises the 
MaxHeapSize
ceiling to 100% of physical memory. Without it, ZGC falls back to the shared heap sizing path and a 25% ceiling. Concurrent preparation still runs, but not the aggressive expansion the measurements depend on.

Using identical memory techniques on every operating system is an explicit non-goal, so large pages may be the default on Linux and not on Windows. The JEP also cautions that applications tuned around a larger initial heap may warm up more slowly and need re-tuning.

Two further edges live in the implementation rather than the text. Pairing 

-XX:+UseLargePages
with adaptive sizing and no 
-Xmx
logs a warning and disables explicit large pages for the heap. The retry loop around 
MADV_COLLAPSE
can also spin indefinitely when 
EAGAIN
persists, a case the code attributes to pinning through 
mlock
or long-term DMA and treats as user error.

Teams can see the heap sizing difference for themselves on the JDK 28 early-access builds by comparing the resolved flags:

$ java -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E "MinHeapSize|InitialHeapSize|MaxHeapSize"
$ java -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZAdaptiveHeapSizing -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E "MinHeapSize|InitialHeapSize|MaxHeapSize"

The second run drops the minimum and initial sizes to the 2 MB floor and lifts the maximum from a quarter of physical memory to all of it. Adding 

-Xlog:gc+init
reports 
Memory Heating: Enabled
and, once the collapse path is active, 
Large Page Support: Enabled (Transparent, JVM enforced)
.

Services already running a modest heap on Linux 6.1 or later pick up concurrent pre-touch and background large pages without touching a flag, because memory heating is on by default. Services carrying a large pre-touched heap purely to buy warmup have something to delete, though only after enabling adaptive sizing. That 100% ceiling reads worse than it behaves. The policy tracks machine-wide memory and holds a reserve, preferring to leave a fifth of the machine free, fighting for a tenth and enforcing a twentieth, with those margins widening when usage is unstable or compressed.

JDK 28 reaches Rampdown Phase One on December 3, 2026, with general availability scheduled for March 9, 2027. The JEP's own future work points at better CPU sharing between concurrent collection and concurrent commit, and at ahead-of-time compilation from JEP 544, already Completed for JDK 28, which frees JIT cycles the memory workers could spend instead.

entries.title: Java News Roundup: Java4Shell, Oracle CSPUs, OpenJDK, Azul Payara, BellSoft, Helidon, LangChain4j
entries.summary: This week's Java roundup for November 16th, 2026, features news highlighting: the Java4Shell RCE vulnerability; Oracle CSPUs; Lazy Constants targeted for JDK 28; the November 2026 edition of Azul Payara; point releases of Java Operator SDK, LangChain4j and Micrometer; maintenance releases of Liberica JDK and Helidon; and second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive. By Michael Redlich
entries.content:
This week's Java roundup for November 16th, 2026, features news highlighting: the Java4Shell RCE vulnerability; Oracle CSPUs; Lazy Constants targeted for JDK 28; the November 2026 edition of Azul Payara; point releases of Java Operator SDK, LangChain4j and Micrometer; maintenance releases of Liberica JDK and Helidon; and second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive.

OpenJDK

Oracle has released versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3, 11.0.33.0.3 and 8u511b3 of the JDK as part of their quarterly Critical Security Patch Update Advisory for November 2026. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes for version 27.0.1.0.3, version 25.0.5.0.3, version 21.0.13.0.3, version 17.0.21.0.3, version 11.0.33.0.3 and version 8u511 b33.

JEP 547, Lazy Constants (Fourth Preview), has been elevated from Proposed to Target to Targeted for JDK 28. This JEP proposes a fourth preview, with no changes, after three rounds of preview delivered in the upcoming release of JDK 27 and JDK 26 through JDK 25. Formerly known as Stable Values and Computed Constants, this feature introduces the concept of computed constants, defined as immutable value holders that are initialized at most once. This offers the performance and safety benefits of 

final
fields, while offering greater flexibility as to the timing of initialization. The name change from Stable Values to Lazy Constants with the release of JDK 26, better captures the intent of a high-level use case.

JEP 548, Vector API (Thirteenth Incubator), has been elevated from its JEP Draft 8397768 to Candidate status. This JEP proposes a thirteenth incubation with one notable change, after twelve rounds of incubation delivered in JDK 16 through JDK 27. This feature introduces an API to "express vector computations that reliably compile at runtime to optimal vector instructions on supported CPU architectures, thus achieving performance superior to equivalent scalar computations." This JEP adds support for 

 vectors, whose lanes hold 16-bit floating-point numbers in the IEEE 754 Vector
binary16
 format. The Vector API will continue to incubate until the necessary features of Project Valhalla become available as preview features. At that time, the Vector API team will adapt the Vector API and its implementation to use them, and will promote the Vector API from Incubation to Preview.
    
JDK 28

    
Build 25 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 24 that include fixes for various issues. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

    
For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.

    
Java4Shell

    
A new Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability, known as Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), affects versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3 and 8u511b33-perf of Oracle Java SE, versions 21.0.13.0.3 and 17.0.21.0.3 of Oracle GraalVM for JDK, and Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition: 21.3.20.0.3. As described in the CVE documentation:

    


[This] difficult to exploit vulnerability allows [an] unauthenticated attacker with network access via multiple protocols to compromise Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Note: This vulnerability can only be exploited by supplying data to APIs in the specified Component without using Untrusted Java Web Start applications or Untrusted Java applets, such as through a web service.

    
Organizations and projects that have addressed this CVE include: BellSoft, Azul, JetBrains, GraalVM, Quarkus and WildFly. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.

    
Spring Framework

    
It was a busy week over at Spring as the various teams have delivered GA releases that include: Spring Boot, Spring Framework, Spring Security, Spring Session, Spring Integration, Spring HATEOAS, Spring Modulith, Spring AI, Spring AMQP, Spring for Apache Kafka and Spring LDAP.

    
The Spring team has also resolved a total of 90 CVEs spanning multiple projects. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.

    
Azul Payara

    
The release of Azul Payara 7.6.0, the November 2026 edition, includes Community Edition 7.2026.11, Enterprise Edition 6.44.0 and Enterprise Edition 5.93.0. Along with bug fixes and component upgrades, all three editions deliver resolutions to five CVEs, two of which are related to Azul Payara:

    
    
      
  • CVE-2026-90908, a vulnerability in the 
    GenericAdminAuthenticator
     class that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to bypass JMX/RMI administrative access restrictions by spoofing the client host address that may lead to remote code execution.
    • 
      
  • CVE-2026-110003, A vulnerability in the administration REST interface that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to bypass secure-admin remote-access restrictions by supplying an arbitrary value in the 
    X-GlassFish-authToken
     HTTP header that grants execution of arbitrary administrative commands, equivalent to complete compromise of the server.
    • 
    

    
Further details on this release may be found in the release notes and the Azul Payara security advisories page.

    
Hibernate

    
The second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive 5.1.0 and 5.0.0 ship with one single bug fix from the first release candidates, in which use of the Jakarta Persistence 
 annotation could cause a deadlock when a session holding the lock on the row of the generator table needed a new block of IDs.@TableGenerator
    
Version 5.0.0.CR2 will be the last release candidate. With the GA release of version 5.0.0.Final, it will be declared as end-of-life and focus will be on version 5.1.0.

    
More details on these releases may be found in the release notes for version 5.1.0.CR2 and version 5.0.0.CR2.

    
Java Operator SDK

    
The release of Java Operator SDK 5.7.0 provides bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: the ability to enable virtual threads via construction in the 
 class or the Operator
josdk.use-virtual-threads
 property; and a new 
keepAlive()
 method, defined in the 
Operator
 class that starts a non-daemon thread to keep the JVM running until the operator is shut down. Version 5.7 is now built on Fabric8 Kubernetes Client 8.0. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.
    
BellSoft

    
Concurrent with Oracle's Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU) for November 2026, BellSoft has released CSPU patches for versions 27.0.1.1 25.0.5.1, 21.0.13.1, 17.0.21.1, 11.0.33.1, 8u514 7u523 and 6u523 of Liberica JDK, their downstream distribution of OpenJDK, to address this list of CVEs. This release also includes a patch for the aforementioned Java4Shell Remote Code Execution vulnerability.

    
With an overall total of 111 fixes and backports, BellSoft states they have participated in eliminating 21 issues in all releases.

    
Helidon

    
The release of Helidon 27.0.2 delivers bug fixes and one notable change in which the default limit of decoded-input (strings, byte arrays, JSON, forms, and buffered multipart parts) for in-memory entity conversations has been increased to 1 mebibyte (MiB). More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

    
This release also aligns with the Oracle Critical Patch Updates for November 2026 and includes the Helidon 4.x and 3.x release trains as described in this blog post.

    
LangChain4j

    
The formal release (along with the thirty-fourth beta release) of LangChain4j 1.24.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: new 
 and DecisionSchedulerPlanner
 classes to serve as a decision model-based agentic pattern; and support for resuming suspended agentic systems in the DecisionModels
 class. Further details on this release, including breaking changes, may be found in the AgentMonitorrelease notes.
    
Micrometer

    
After two milestones and two releases candidates, the GA release of Micrometer Metrics 1.18.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: an optimization of the 
 and PrometheusMeterRegistry
 classes for collecting data snapshots; and a new MicrometerCollector
RowState
 inner class, defined in the 
 class, that eliminates the need to remove and re-register an instance of the existing MultiGauge
Row
 inner class. More details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the release notes.
    
Similarly, the GA release of Micrometer Tracing 1.8.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a simplification of baggage handles and lookups by directly storing the name of the handle and its metadata by eliminating use of the 
CompositeBaggage
 and Java 
 classes; and a refactor of the AtomicReference
 class for improved baggage propagation. Further details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the BaggageTextMapPropagatorrelease notes.

entries.title: Netflix at QConSF 2026: Retrofitting the SDLC for AI Coding Agents
entries.summary: At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mark Khuzam of Netflix explained how the Commerce team retrofitted its SDLC so AI coding agents and engineers could ship together. The team wrote 45 architecture decision records for people and agents, added a review agent that posts only verified blockers, and serves per-domain GraphRAG context through a single MCP tool. By Andrew Hoblitzell
entries.content:
At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mark Khuzam, senior software engineer at Netflix, described how the company's Commerce team retrofitted its software development lifecycle so that AI coding agents and engineers could ship together safely.

Khuzam argued that most of the work was not about agents at all, but about documentation, consistency and review.

Much of Commerce runs as server-driven UI, an approach Netflix has discussed at QCon before. A single screen-composition service behind the API gateway builds screens for iOS, Android, web and TV.

Khuzam opened with a mock company email announcing that every engineer now had Claude Code and asking how much faster everyone was shipping. The problem the team ran into next was summed up in one line.

Agents promised speed. But we spent 20 years building for humans.

The team's first attempt was having an agent migrate tests, and it took four tries. The team started with "migrate this file," then added instructions, then the APIs to use, then how to mock data.

The docs were also hard to find, since the agent's context window ran out before it found the right page. And they were inconsistent, because tests were not written the same way across the codebase.

Developers rated the internal framework at a Net Promoter Score of -3. Moving from one test to a whole feature, from screen to data to route to test, meant teaching the agent how the team builds.

Khuzam described the fix as context engineering, "getting what engineers know into what agents see." The team wrote 45 architecture decision records, each "written for people and for agents."

Each record covers the context, the decision, a pattern and an anti-pattern, and AI usage notes on what an agent should do. It also links to related docs and code, and the records now ship inside almost every repository.

To keep those records and more than 300 other documents findable, the team borrowed from how search engines read a site. An AGENTS.md file, the project instructions file that coding agents read before anything else, plays the part of robots.txt.

The second half of the talk followed code after an agent writes it. Khuzam noted that the CI pipeline is still deterministic, running builds, tests, screenshot diffing, merge queues and canaries.

What changed is how agents plug into each phase. A review agent pre-reviews each pull request against the docs and ADRs, flags anti-patterns and looks at what depends on the change.

Its first version left 23 comments on a single PR, starting with "Overall this PR looks great!" It now posts only verified blockers, each with evidence, a fix and the ADR rule it breaks. Engineers can add a revise label to have an agent read the review and push a fix to the same PR. Changes aren't yet auto-merged, and engineers own the code.

Khuzam reported no Sev 1 incidents in 2026 on a core service and 32% more pull requests year over year. Developer NPS rose from -3 to +25 over three quarters.

Ahead of the session, Khuzam framed the stakes on LinkedIn: "Agents can write code, but what gives us the confidence to ship Tier 0 services to 300M+ members without everything falling apart?"

Work that crosses services raised a harder question. A product engineer building one feature touches the payment API, billing, the gateway and every client, so the team had to decide who owns the context and how it follows the work.

Khuzam listed approaches that did not hold up. Loading every repository did not fit, Git submodules were brittle, a Git MCP server "sees one file, not the system," and shared copies went stale.

The team needed context that was accurate, portable across agents, owned per domain and kept fresh. It settled on GraphRAG per domain, taking structure from the code and meaning from the docs and ADRs.

Each graph is pinned to specific commits and served through a single Model Context Protocol tool. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, a Slack bot and CI review all query the same graph, and every answer cites a file and a line.

Khuzam closed with three rules: decide what agents should do and tell them, make it easy to find how to do it, and remember that human judgement still matters. "None of this is new. It's good engineering, built for a new reader."

Developers interested in learning more can watch InfoQ in the coming weeks for video of the session and can view the session details here.
